views.name: film_basic
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  film_id,
  title,
  description,
  release_year,
  language_id,
  original_language_id,
  rental_duration,
  rental_rate,
  length,
  replacement_cost,
  rating,
  special_features,
  last_update
FROM film

params.when_to_use: retrieve one row per film with its core attributes (film_id, title, description, release_year, language ids, duration/rate/length/cost, rating, special_features, last_update). | look up film metadata for display, linking, or joining to other tables at the film grain (e.g., show film details on a product page). | filter or search films by any of the listed columns while preserving one-row-per-film semantics (e.g., find films released in 2006 or films with rating = 'PG'). | build downstream joins or aggregations that need the canonical film-level attributes as the base table (for example, counting rentals per film after joining to rental or inventory).
params.when_not_to_use: answer questions that require counts, aggregates, or summaries (e.g., 'how many times was each film rented?') — film_basic is one row per film and contains no rental/inventory aggregation, so reusing it will undercount or return zero counts unless you join to aggregation sources. | compute per-store or per-inventory metrics (e.g., 'inventory available by store' or 'rentals per store') — grain mismatch: film_basic is at film_id grain, not inventory_id or store_id, so using it will hide multiplicity and produce silently incorrect results. | derive cast or category cohorts (e.g., 'all films featuring actor X' or 'films in category Y') — film_basic lacks actor/category relationships; reusing it without joining the appropriate join tables will return incorrect cohorts (false negatives). | produce customer- or payment-level analytics (e.g., 'revenue per customer' or 'customer lifetime value features') — these are at customer/payment grain and require joining to payment/rental/inventory tables; film_basic has no transactional columns and will misrepresent totals. | use as a de-duplicated source when you actually need row-level rental or inventory detail — reuse will silently drop multiplicity (e.g., joining film_basic to rental and aggregating without accounting for rental rows duplicates film attributes but not the rental counts unless join keys and aggregation are handled correctly).
params.comparison: use film_category_join instead when you need film-level rows augmented with category membership — film_basic has film attributes only, while film_category_join includes category relationships so it preserves film-to-category linkage for cohort/segmentation queries. | use film_actor_join instead when you need film-level rows augmented with actor membership — film_basic will not provide actor associations; film_actor_join exposes film-to-actor links needed to list cast or filter by actor. | use inventory_by_film_store instead when you need inventory counts or availability per film per store — inventory_by_film_store is an aggregation at (film_id, store_id) or similar and preserves multiplicity by store that film_basic does not. | use film_rental_counts instead when you need pre-aggregated rental counts per film — film_basic has no rental metrics, whereas film_rental_counts provides counts so you avoid miscounting by joining raw rental rows yourself. | use rental_enriched or payment_by_customer when your analysis depends on transactional data (rentals/payments) or customer-level aggregations — these siblings bring the transactional grain and metrics that film_basic lacks. | use ranked_films_by_rentals when you want films ordered or ranked by popularity/usage metrics — film_basic provides only static attributes and cannot be used to rank films by rental activity without additional aggregation.

views.description: Normalized film master rows with key descriptive attributes and canonical numeric measures. Useful as the base film dimension for joins, filtering, and aggregations (e.g., revenue by film, film counts by rating/category). | Use for: List films with attributes; join to categories/actors/inventory; Filter films by rating, language, release_year, or length; Use rental_rate or replacement_cost in aggregations

views.name: film_category_join
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  f.film_id,
  f.title,
  f.release_year,
  f.language_id,
  f.rental_rate,
  f.length,
  fc.category_id,
  c.name AS name,
  fc.last_update AS last_update
FROM film_category fc
JOIN film f ON fc.film_id = f.film_id
JOIN category c ON fc.category_id = c.category_id

params.when_to_use: List or inspect film-to-category membership at the film-category grain (one row per film_id × category_id). | Join film attributes (title, release_year, language_id, rental_rate, length) to category metadata for analyses that need the category of each specific film copy (e.g., catalog browsing, category-level tagging). | Filter or aggregate after joining at the film×category level (for example: count films per category by counting distinct film_id from this view). | Produce datasets where you need the exact film_category.last_update timestamp per film×category association.
params.when_not_to_use: Do not use when you need one row per film only (film-level grain). Using this view and then aggregating without DISTINCT may double-count films that belong to multiple categories. | Do not use for inventory- or stock-level questions (e.g., number of physical copies or availability). This view is at film×category and does not contain inventory_id, store_id, or copy-level rows used by inventory_by_film_store or inventory tables—using it will undercount or miss store-level variation. | Do not use when you need rental or revenue metrics (counts, sums) directly. This view contains no rental or payment fields; aggregating its rows does not reflect rental transactions and will lead to silently-wrong metrics. | Do not use when you need customer- or transaction-centered cohorts (customer lifetime, spend, rentals). It has no customer, rental, or payment identifiers; substituting it will drop or misattribute cohorts. | Do not use when you need film ranking by rentals or precomputed rental counts. film_rental_counts and ranked_films_by_rentals already compute per-film rental aggregates; this view will not provide correct counts and will double-count films with multiple categories if naively joined to rentals. | Do not use when you need language or category names normalized from other sources beyond the category.name and film.language_id present here—this view does not include language names, only language_id.
params.comparison: use film_basic instead when you need one row per film (film-level attributes without category). — film_basic has a film-level grain; film_category_join is film×category and will produce multiple rows per film when a film has multiple categories. | use inventory_by_film_store instead when you need inventory counts or store-level availability. — inventory_by_film_store aggregates inventory per film and store; film_category_join has no inventory identifiers and cannot represent stock. | use film_rental_counts or ranked_films_by_rentals instead when you need rental counts or rankings. — those siblings produce pre-aggregated rental metrics per film (and ranking), whereas film_category_join only links films to categories and will not provide rental metrics and can cause double-counting if joined incorrectly. | use rental_enriched or payment_by_customer when you need transaction-level rental/payment data or customer cohorts. — rental_enriched and payment_by_customer include transactional identifiers and monetary fields; film_category_join lacks them and is unsuitable for transaction analysis. | use film_actor_join when you need actor–film relationships. — film_actor_join shares the same pattern (a join table) but for actor associations; choose the join view that matches the association you intend to analyze (actor vs category).

views.description: Denormalized mapping of films to their categories with film descriptive columns. Useful for category-level aggregations, counts, or filtering films by category name. | Use for: Count films per category or list films in a category; Aggregate revenue or rentals by category after joining payments/rentals/inventory; Filter films by category name and other film attributes

views.name: film_actor_join
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  fa.film_id,
  fa.actor_id,
  a.first_name,
  a.last_name,
  f.title,
  f.release_year,
  fa.last_update
FROM film_actor fa
JOIN actor a ON fa.actor_id = a.actor_id
JOIN film f ON fa.film_id = f.film_id

params.when_to_use: List all actor–film pairings with actor names and basic film metadata — e.g., “Which actors appear in which films?” at the actor×film grain. | Join to other tables keyed at the same grain (film_id, actor_id) to answer questions about attributes of a specific actor’s participation in a specific film. | Produce detail-level rows for downstream enrichment or filtering (e.g., apply filters to actor or film fields) before aggregating at a different grain.
params.when_not_to_use: Do not use when you need film-level aggregates (e.g., number of distinct actors per film) without explicitly aggregating — the view is at the actor×film grain and will cause overcounting if summed or counted without grouping. | Do not use when you need actor-level aggregates (e.g., total films per actor) without grouping — reusing the view directly will duplicate actor rows across films and yield incorrect counts. | Do not use when you need inventory, rental, payment, or store-level facts — this view contains no inventory, rental, payment, or store measures and reusing it for those questions will produce silently incomplete results. | Do not use when you need film-only dimensional rows (one row per film) such as film_basic — this view repeats film fields for each actor and therefore is the wrong grain for film-level metrics or deduplicated film lists. | Do not use when you need actor-only dimensional rows (one row per actor) such as a distinct actor roster — the view duplicates actor rows per film. | Do not use as a source of temporal or transactional measures (rentals, payments, last rental date, etc.) — last_update here is the film_actor.last_update timestamp and is unrelated to rental/payment events; confusing them leads to wrong temporal analyses.
params.comparison: use film_basic instead when you need one-row-per-film details — film_basic provides film-level normalized attributes without actor duplication. | use film_category_join instead when you need film↔category relationships (film_id-level category context) — film_category_join is the correct join for category membership rather than actor membership. | use inventory_by_film_store when you need aggregated inventory counts by film and store — inventory_by_film_store contains inventory measures and aggregation that film_actor_join does not. | use film_rental_counts or ranked_films_by_rentals when you need rental-based aggregates or rankings — those siblings compute rental counts/ ranks; film_actor_join only provides film–actor links and will not reflect rental metrics. | use customer_contact, customer_ltv_features, payment_by_customer, or rental_enriched when your question concerns customers, payments, or rentals — those views are focused on customer/payment/rental facts, whereas film_actor_join contains no customer/payment/rental data. | use store_staff_manager when you need store/staff hierarchy or manager info — film_actor_join has no store or staff context and is the wrong dimension for such questions.

views.description: Mapping of films to actors with actor name columns and film identifying info. Useful for actor filmographies, counting films per actor, or filtering films by actor. | Use for: List films for a given actor or actors for a given film; Count films per actor or co-actor networks; Filter films by actor attributes combined with film attributes

views.name: inventory_by_film_store
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  film_id,
  store_id,
  COUNT(inventory_id) AS inventory_count
FROM inventory
GROUP BY film_id, store_id

params.when_to_use: When you need the number of inventory items (rows in inventory table) available for each film at each store — i.e., questions like 'How many inventory units of film X are at store Y?' | When joining to other tables at the exact grain film_id + store_id (for example to compute store-level stock availability per film or to compare inventory_count against store capacity) where inventory_count is an input to further aggregations but only if you preserve the film_id+store_id grouping during downstream processing | When computing ratios or metrics that explicitly require the count of inventory records per (film_id, store_id), for example inventory_count / total_inventory_for_store (only after aggregating appropriately)
params.when_not_to_use: When you need inventory counts at a different grain (e.g., per store only, per film only, or per film+language/etc.) — reusing this view and then aggregating without care can double-count or misrepresent the true counts because this view is pre-aggregated at film_id+store_id. | When your question is about distinct physical items (for instance if inventory_id may be duplicated in source or if you need COUNT(DISTINCT inventory_id)) — this view uses COUNT(inventory_id) and will be wrong if deduplication is required. | When you need time- or state-filtered cohorts (e.g., available inventory at a given date, inventory currently rented vs available) — this view aggregates all inventory rows and applies no status or temporal filters, so it will include rented, unavailable, or historical rows unless filtered upstream on raw inventory. | When you need row-level detail (for example to list inventory_id values, rental history, or to join to rental records per inventory item) — this is an aggregate view and loses row-level identifiers. | When combining with sibling aggregates that are at a different grain (e.g., joining to payment_by_customer which is per customer) without first aligning grains — doing so can produce silently-wrong join multiplicity and inflated counts. | When you expect inventory_count to reflect rentals or demand (for example 'times rented') — this view counts inventory rows, not rentals; use film_rental_counts or rental_enriched for rental-based metrics.
params.comparison: use film_rental_counts instead when you want counts of rentals by film (rental event counts) — film_rental_counts aggregates rental activity, whereas inventory_by_film_store counts inventory rows (different measure). | use rental_enriched when you need to relate inventory to rental status, dates, or customer activity — rental_enriched is a join that surfaces rental attributes and temporal context; inventory_by_film_store has no temporal or rental information. | use film_basic when you need film-level attributes (title, description, length, etc.) at the film grain — film_basic is normalized film metadata at film_id grain; inventory_by_film_store is an aggregate at film_id+store_id and will require aggregation to compare at film level. | use payment_by_customer when your analysis is at the customer-payment level — payment_by_customer is an aggregate at customer/payment-related grains, while inventory_by_film_store is an inventory-count aggregate at film+store and not aligned for customer spend analyses. | use customer_ltv_features or customer_contact for customer-centric cohorts — those sibling views expose customer-level features; inventory_by_film_store is unrelated in grain and measure, so substitute only when you change the question to inventory per film/store.

views.description: Inventory counts per film and store (one row per film_id, store_id) with available inventory measure. Useful to join to rentals/payments to compute utilization or to see stock distribution across stores. | Use for: Compute availability or stock per film per store; Join inventory counts to rentals to compute turnover or utilization rates

views.name: rental_enriched
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  r.rental_id,
  r.rental_date,
  r.return_date,
  r.inventory_id,
  inv.film_id,
  inv.store_id,
  r.customer_id,
  r.staff_id,
  r.last_update
FROM rental r
LEFT JOIN inventory inv ON r.inventory_id = inv.inventory_id

params.when_to_use: List or examine individual rental events by rental_id, including rental and return timestamps and the inventory/film/store/customer/staff involved — use when you need one row per rental. | Join into analyses that require the canonical rental-level attributes (rental_date, return_date, inventory_id, customer_id, staff_id) without aggregating — e.g., time-to-return per rental, rental-level filters, or exporting raw rental records. | Filter or slice rentals by inventory, film, store, customer, or staff and then perform your own aggregations at the desired level (because the view preserves rental-level detail).
params.when_not_to_use: Do not use to answer questions that expect film- or store-level aggregates (e.g., total rentals per film or rentals per store) without performing an explicit GROUP BY — reusing it directly for aggregate counts risks double-counting because the view is at the rental_id grain. | Do not use as a source of customer lifetime metrics or per-customer summaries without aggregating by customer_id first — the view contains one row per rental, so queries that forget to group will produce rental-level results, not customer-level summaries. | Do not use to get inventory-only or film-only records independent of rentals — because this is a LEFT JOIN from rental to inventory, inventory rows with no rentals are absent; conversely, inventory fields are NULL only if a rental references a missing inventory row (rare), so it does not represent the inventory universe. | Do not use when you need only payments or payment-derived metrics — payments are a different domain (see payment_by_customer); joining payments to this view without care can change row multiplicity (a one-to-many relationship between rentals and payments may exist in your schema). | Do not assume nullability or completeness for inventory fields: inventory-derived columns (film_id, store_id) come from the LEFT JOIN; if inventory is missing, those columns will be NULL. Using this view for inner-join semantics on inventory would silently include rentals with missing inventory unless you explicitly filter. | Do not use for ranked or pre-aggregated film ranking queries — this view is not aggregated or ranked; reusing it in place of ranked_films_by_rentals or film_rental_counts will require aggregation and ranking logic to be added, otherwise results will be incorrect.
params.comparison: use film_basic instead when you need canonical film attributes (one row per film) — film_basic is normalized to film grain, whereas rental_enriched is at rental grain and will produce many rows per film. | use inventory_by_film_store instead when you need aggregated inventory counts per film/store — inventory_by_film_store is pre-aggregated for that purpose; rental_enriched contains every rental and will require grouping to match that aggregation. | use payment_by_customer instead when you need customer payment aggregates or lifetime value inputs — payment_by_customer is aggregated on customer and monetary metrics; rental_enriched is rental-level and excludes payment-specific columns. | use customer_ltv_features when you need precomputed customer-level lifetime features — customer_ltv_features is already aggregated per customer; rental_enriched would require careful aggregation to produce equivalent features and risks mis-counts if joins are added without grouping. | use film_rental_counts or ranked_films_by_rentals when you need counts or rankings of films by rental activity — those sibling views already compute counts/ranks at the film grain; rental_enriched must be aggregated and ranked to serve the same purpose and could mislead if used directly.

views.description: Event-level rentals enriched with customer, inventory, film and store identifiers and rental timing. Useful for time-based analyses, lifetime metrics, and joining to payments. | Use for: Calculate rental durations, on-time returns, or active rentals over time; Join rentals to payments or customers for revenue and retention analyses

views.name: payment_by_customer
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  customer_id,
  COUNT(payment_id) AS payment_count,
  SUM(amount) AS payment_total,
  MIN(payment_date) AS first_payment_date,
  MAX(payment_date) AS last_payment_date
FROM payment
GROUP BY customer_id

params.when_to_use: Compute per-customer payment summaries over the entire payments table (e.g., "how many payments and total amount has each customer ever made?"). | Join to customer-level tables where one row per customer is required (e.g., enrich customer profile with their total payments and first/last payment dates). | Build customer lifetime value or retention features that require counts, sums, and first/last payment timestamps at the customer grain.
params.when_not_to_use: As a source for payment-level analysis (anti-pattern: expecting row-level payments). This view is aggregated to customer granularity and loses individual payment rows (you will silently miscount or cannot access payment_id-level detail). | When asking for time-windowed cohorts (anti-pattern: expecting a filtered time period). The view aggregates across all time; using it for a specific period without recomputing or filtering at the payment level can produce incorrect counts/totals because first_payment_date/last_payment_date reflect all payments, not the cohort window. | When computing per-customer-per-period (e.g., monthly) metrics (anti-pattern: expecting lower-level period granularity). The view has one row per customer only and cannot represent multiple periods per customer. | When counting distinct payments by some attribute other than payment_id (anti-pattern: expecting deduplication or different count semantics). The view uses COUNT(payment_id) and SUM(amount) over all payments — if you need COUNT(DISTINCT ...) or conditional sums, re-aggregate from payment. | When using the view to filter customers by whether they made a payment in a given timeframe (anti-pattern: using first_payment_date/last_payment_date as a replacement for filtered aggregation). Because first/last are across all time, selecting customers where last_payment_date >= X does not equal aggregating payments only in a window and may misclassify customers who have payments outside the window. | When joining to produce metrics at a different grain (e.g., film or store) where payments should be apportioned per rental/film/store (anti-pattern: aggregating at customer then joining to lower-grain entity). Aggregating before correct joins can cause double-counting or wrong attribution.
params.comparison: use customer_ltv_features instead when you need precomputed customer-level LTV/feature set — it is also an AGG at customer grain but likely contains additional engineered fields (so prefer it if it provides the specific features you need). | use rental_enriched or film_rental_counts instead when you need payment or revenue metrics tied to rentals, films, or stores — those sibling views join payment/rental/film/inventory context so they preserve correct attribution at those grains (this view only aggregates by customer). | use payment (base table) instead of this view when you need row-level payment details, conditional counts, or time-windowed aggregations — the base table preserves payment_id, payment_date, amount and allows correct re-aggregation for different cohorts or grains.

views.description: Aggregated payment amounts and counts per customer (one row per customer) for customer-level revenue analysis and LTV-style metrics. | Use for: Compute revenue per customer, frequency, and recency; Segment customers by payment_total or activity

views.name: customer_contact
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  c.customer_id,
  c.store_id,
  c.first_name,
  c.last_name,
  c.email,
  c.address_id,
  a.address,
  a.address2,
  a.district,
  a.city_id,
  ct.city,
  ct.country_id,
  co.country,
  a.postal_code,
  a.phone,
  c.active,
  c.create_date,
  c.last_update
FROM customer c
LEFT JOIN address a ON c.address_id = a.address_id
LEFT JOIN city ct ON a.city_id = ct.city_id
LEFT JOIN country co ON ct.country_id = co.country_id

params.when_to_use: Lookup customer-level contact and location attributes for each customer_id (e.g., mailing label, email/phone, city/country names). | Joining a customers table to addresses/cities/countries when you need denormalized customer contact fields at the customer grain (one row per customer). | Producing downstream features or exports that require the customer's address and contact details without additional aggregation or filtering (e.g., generate shipping labels, contact lists). | Enriching customer records before joining to transactional tables where you will preserve the one-row-per-customer cardinality (e.g., join to payments or rentals on customer_id afterwards).
params.when_not_to_use: Do not reuse when you need a different grain than customer_id (e.g., store-level summaries or per-address aggregates). This view is one row per customer; aggregating without adjusting for possible NULL addresses can miscount customers or addresses. | Avoid for cohort or time-windowed analyses that require filtering by create_date or last_update before joins — the view exposes those timestamps but does not implement cohort selection; applying filters after joining other tables may change join cardinality and produce incorrect cohorts. | Do not use as a source when you need ONLY active customers or ONLY customers with non-null email/phone — the view includes all customers (LEFT JOIN to address preserves customers with missing address fields). Reusing it will silently include customers missing contact/location data unless you explicitly filter. | Avoid using it as a pre-aggregated source for counts or sums (e.g., customers per city) without verifying duplicates or NULL city_id handling. Because address and city are joined via LEFT JOINs, city and country fields can be NULL; naive COUNTs may yield unexpected zeros or mis-attributed rows. | Not appropriate when you need transactional enrichment (payments, rentals) already joined and aggregated by customer — other sibling views provide aggregated or enriched transaction data required for metrics like LTV or rental totals.
params.comparison: use customer_ltv_features instead when you need customer-level aggregated transaction metrics (LTV, total_spend, counts) — it has the same customer grain but additionally aggregates payment/rental history so you won't need to re-aggregate transactions yourself. | use payment_by_customer instead when your goal is metrics about customer payments (sums, counts, times) — it is an AGG view already aggregated by customer and avoids mis-aggregating payments if you attempted to derive them from this join-only view. | use rental_enriched instead when you need customer rows enriched with rental/payment transaction context — rental_enriched includes transaction joins/fields so you won't have to join transactional tables separately and risk changing cardinality. | use store_staff_manager when you are combining store or staff managerial info with customers (store-level joins) — that sibling provides joins targeted at store/staff relationships rather than purely customer contact/location attributes. | use inventory_by_film_store, film_rental_counts, or ranked_films_by_rentals for film or store-level aggregation/ranking tasks — those siblings are AGG or RANK views tailored to aggregated counts and rankings; reusing customer_contact for such tasks would be the wrong grain and produce silently incorrect results.

views.description: Customer rows with address, city and country descriptive columns for geographic segmentation and contact-level attributes. | Use for: Geographic distribution of customers, mailing lists, or contact-based filters; Join customers to payments/rentals to compute regional metrics

views.name: customer_ltv_features
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  c.customer_id,
  COALESCE(p.payment_count,0) AS payment_count,
  COALESCE(p.payment_total,0.0) AS payment_total,
  CASE WHEN COALESCE(p.payment_count,0)>0 THEN (p.payment_total / p.payment_count) ELSE 0.0 END AS avg_payment,
  COALESCE(r.rental_count,0) AS rental_count,
  COALESCE(r.first_rental_date, NULL) AS first_rental_date,
  COALESCE(r.last_rental_date, NULL) AS last_rental_date
FROM customer c
LEFT JOIN (
  SELECT customer_id, COUNT(payment_id) AS payment_count, SUM(amount) AS payment_total
  FROM payment
  GROUP BY customer_id
) p ON c.customer_id = p.customer_id
LEFT JOIN (
  SELECT customer_id, COUNT(rental_id) AS rental_count, MIN(rental_date) AS first_rental_date, MAX(rental_date) AS last_rental_date
  FROM rental
  GROUP BY customer_id
) r ON c.customer_id = r.customer_id

params.when_to_use: Compute per-customer lifetime totals and counts: e.g. "for each customer, what is their total payment amount, number of payments, number of rentals, and first/last rental dates?" | Join customer-level attributes to these LTV features when you need one row per customer (customer-level reporting, cohorting by customer attributes). | Surface simple averages per customer such as avg_payment computed as payment_total / payment_count (note: zero when no payments). | Build downstream customer-level models or dashboards that expect exactly one row per customer, including customers with zero payments or zero rentals (LEFT JOIN ensures all customers appear).
params.when_not_to_use: Do not reuse when you need a different grain (e.g., rental-level, payment-level, film-level, store-level or customer+film): this view is strictly one row per customer; using it for lower-grain analytics will silently hide multiplicity and undercount rows. | Do not reuse when you need cohort-restricted aggregations (e.g., payments only in a date range or only for a particular store or film): the view aggregates across the entire payment and rental tables with no filters, so it cannot represent time-windowed or filtered cohorts — reusing it will return wrong totals. | Do not reuse for rate or frequency metrics requiring a defined exposure window (e.g., payments per month since first rental): avg_payment here is payment_total/payment_count and rental_count is a lifetime count; exposure/time-normalized metrics will be incorrect if you assume time scaling. | Do not reuse when you require distinct-count semantics for payments or rentals in presence of joins elsewhere: payment_count and rental_count are simple COUNTs grouped by customer; if downstream joins duplicate payments/rentals, using these pre-aggregates can produce double-counting or misalignment. | Do not reuse for analyses that expect NULLs instead of zeros to indicate absence: payment_count/payment_total are coerced to 0 via COALESCE, so you cannot distinguish "no payments recorded" from "zero-valued payments" without re-querying source tables. | Do not reuse when you need transactional detail (payment_id, rental_id, payment_date, film_id, store_id, staff_id): this view contains only counts, totals, and first/last rental dates and will silently drop necessary identifiers and timestamps.
params.comparison: use payment_by_customer instead when you need the same customer-level payment aggregates but want a view focused only on payments — it may differ in how NULLs/zeros are handled or in included columns; payment_by_customer will be a more explicit source for payment-only cohorts and may be faster if you don't need rental info. | use rental_enriched instead when you need rental-level detail or to join rentals to films/stores/staff — rental_enriched is a JOIN-level view that preserves rental rows and related attributes, whereas customer_ltv_features collapses rentals to per-customer counts and min/max dates (lossy for rental detail). | use inventory_by_film_store or film_rental_counts when you need film- or store-level aggregations — those sibling AGG views aggregate at a different grain (film or inventory/store) and are appropriate for film/store questions; reusing customer_ltv_features for film/store questions will be mismatched by grain. | use customer_contact when you need customer-level joins to contact or demographic fields without aggregated LTV metrics — customer_contact is a JOIN view focused on customer metadata, while customer_ltv_features mixes customer metadata (customer_id) with lifetime aggregates; pick the view that matches whether you need raw contact fields or aggregated metrics. | use ranked_films_by_rentals when you need ranked film metrics — ranked_films_by_rentals produces ranking at the film level and has different sorting/aggregation semantics; customer_ltv_features cannot substitute for ranking or film-level leaderboards.

views.description: Customer-level summarized features combining payments and rentals: counts and totals for payments and rentals along with average payment amount. Useful for churn/LTV modeling and segmentation. | Use for: Build features for customer lifetime value or churn models; Segment customers by engagement or revenue metrics

views.name: store_staff_manager
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  s.store_id,
  s.manager_staff_id,
  s.address_id,
  a.address,
  a.address2,
  a.district,
  a.city_id,
  ct.city,
  ct.country_id,
  co.country,
  s.last_update
FROM store s
LEFT JOIN address a ON s.address_id = a.address_id
LEFT JOIN city ct ON a.city_id = ct.city_id
LEFT JOIN country co ON ct.country_id = co.country_id

params.when_to_use: When you need one row per store (grain = store_id) containing the store's current manager_staff_id and the store's mailing address and geographic names (address, address2, district, city, country) as stored in the referenced address/city/country tables. | When you want to enrich store-level data (store_id) with human-readable location fields for reporting, labeling, or joining to other store-level datasets where duplicates per store are not expected. | When you need to show or export store contact/location info (e.g., for a store directory or management assignment list) and the natural primary key is store_id.
params.when_not_to_use: Do not use this view when you need a different grain than store_id — e.g., queries that must be per-address, per-city, per-country, per-staff, per-inventory-item, per-rental, or per-customer. This view returns exactly one row per store (LEFT JOINs may still produce NULLs for missing address/city/country) and will silently drop/divide records if you expect multiple addresses or many-to-many relationships. | Avoid using this view for cohort or temporal analyses that require historic addresses, manager assignments over time, or changes — the view exposes only the current store.manager_staff_id and store.last_update; it does not preserve history or multiple manager assignments. | Do not reuse it when you need counts or aggregations (e.g., number of staff at a store, number of inventories, rental counts) because it contains no aggregated measures and will undercount or misrepresent those metrics if aggregated without joining the correct detail tables first. | Do not assume manager_staff_id implies a staff row exists: manager_staff_id is taken directly from store and the join chain is only to address/city/country; there is no join to the staff table here, so staff attributes (name, email, active flag) are not available and must not be expected. | Avoid using this view to filter on city or country and then count stores without carefully handling NULLs from the LEFT JOINs. Because address/city/country are left-joined, stores with missing address/city/country will still appear; filtering by city.country may unintentionally exclude or include stores if you don't convert NULLs appropriately.
params.comparison: use customer_contact instead when you need contact details tied to customers (customer-level grain) — customer_contact is at the customer grain and includes customer-specific contact fields, whereas store_staff_manager is at the store grain and contains only store location and manager ids. | use rental_enriched instead when you need rental-level details or to analyze rentals by store — rental_enriched is at the rental/inventory grain and contains rental dates and customer/staff relationships; store_staff_manager lacks rental or inventory columns and will not support correct rental-level joins or aggregations. | use inventory_by_film_store when you need counts of inventory per film and store — inventory_by_film_store is an aggregation across inventory rows and returns counts; store_staff_manager has no inventory or counts and aggregating it will produce incorrect inventory metrics. | use payment_by_customer or customer_ltv_features when you need aggregated financials or lifetime value per customer — those sibling views are pre-aggregated at the customer grain, while store_staff_manager is store-grained and will not correctly represent customer-level aggregates. | use film_basic or film_actor_join when your question concerns film attributes or film-to-actor relationships — these are film-grain or film-join views; the store view has different keys and columns and cannot replace film-focused siblings. | use ranked_films_by_rentals or film_rental_counts when you need film rental rankings/counts — those views are aggregated or ranked by film; store_staff_manager does not contain rental counts or film identifiers and would be the wrong source.

views.description: Store-level rows with manager staff info and address for store-level reporting and geographic joins. | Use for: Report sales or rentals by store location; Associate store manager or store geography with performance

views.name: film_rental_counts
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  inv.film_id,
  COUNT(r.rental_id) AS rental_count,
  MIN(r.rental_date) AS first_rental_date,
  MAX(r.rental_date) AS last_rental_date
FROM rental r
JOIN inventory inv ON r.inventory_id = inv.inventory_id
GROUP BY inv.film_id

params.when_to_use: Count total rentals per film across the entire rental table (answering: "How many times has each film been rented overall?") | Get the first and last rental timestamps for each film (answering: "When was each film first/last rented?") | Join to other film-grain objects (film_id as primary key) to enrich film-level metrics (e.g., combine with film_basic by film_id)
params.when_not_to_use: Do not use when you need counts by store, by customer, or by inventory item — this view is aggregated to the film_id grain only, so it collapses all stores and inventory units and will hide store-level or inventory-level differences. | Do not use for time-windowed cohorts (e.g., rentals in the last 30 days) because the view contains the full-history aggregation; filtering this view by rental_date is impossible (rental_date columns are already aggregated to min/max) and would produce incorrect results. | Do not use when you need distinct counts of customers who rented a film — rental_count is COUNT(rental_id), not COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id), so reuse would over-count if multiple rentals by the same customer should be counted once. | Do not use when you need detailed rental rows or attributes (rental_id, customer_id, return_date, staff_id, inventory_id). The view loses row-level detail required for event-level analysis. | Do not use when you require accurate aggregation after additional joins to rental-related tables that change multiplicity (e.g., joining payments or returns without re-aggregating). Because rental_count is pre-aggregated, joining then summing can double-count unless you join only on film_id and trust the pre-aggregated number. | Do not use when you need first/last rental by store or by customer — first_rental_date and last_rental_date are computed across all rentals for the film and will be incorrect for per-store or per-customer inquiries.
params.comparison: use film_basic instead when you need non-aggregated film attributes (title, description, release_year) — film_basic is at the film grain with film metadata rather than rental metrics. | use inventory_by_film_store instead when you need rentals or inventory metrics at the film+store grain — inventory_by_film_store is aggregated with store context and preserves store-level counts that film_rental_counts collapses. | use rental_enriched instead when you need row-level rental details or to compute alternative aggregates (e.g., distinct customers, time-windowed counts) — rental_enriched is a JOIN that retains rental-level columns required for re-aggregation. | use ranked_films_by_rentals when you need an ordered ranking of films by recent rental popularity — ranked_films_by_rentals likely computes a rank and may apply different filters or time windows suited for ranking rather than raw lifetime counts. | use payment_by_customer or customer_ltv_features when your downstream question is about customer monetary metrics — those sibling views are customer-aggregated and include payment information that film_rental_counts does not contain.

views.description: Counts of rentals per film (aggregated from rental->inventory->film) with first/last rental dates. Useful for popularity metrics and trend analyses. | Use for: Rank films by number of rentals or measure popularity; Combine with inventory to compute turnover

views.name: ranked_films_by_rentals
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  fr.film_id,
  fr.rental_count,
  fr.first_rental_date,
  fr.last_rental_date,
  RANK() OVER (ORDER BY fr.rental_count DESC) AS rentals_rank
FROM (
  SELECT
    inv.film_id,
    COUNT(r.rental_id) AS rental_count,
    MIN(r.rental_date) AS first_rental_date,
    MAX(r.rental_date) AS last_rental_date
  FROM rental r
  JOIN inventory inv ON r.inventory_id = inv.inventory_id
  GROUP BY inv.film_id
) fr

params.when_to_use: When you need per-film aggregate rental metrics across the entire rental table: total number of rentals (rental_count), date of first rental (first_rental_date), date of last rental (last_rental_date), and a global rank of films by total rentals (rentals_rank). | When the question’s grain is exactly a single row per film (film_id) and you do not need to filter or partition by store, customer, time window, or other dimensions. | When you want a stable global ranking (RANK()) of films by their overall rental_count (ties receive same rank) and accept that the rank is computed over the entire dataset with DESC ordering on rental_count.
params.when_not_to_use: Do not reuse this view when you need metrics at any finer grain than film (for example per film per store, per film per month, per film per customer). This view aggregates over all rentals for each film, so reusing it for a finer-grained report will silently hide variation (missing rows or duplicated film-level values) and produce incorrectly aggregated results. | Do not use it when you need counts or dates limited to a cohort or time window (for example rentals in 2020, or rentals since a promotion). The view’s rental_count, first_rental_date and last_rental_date are computed over all rows in rental and will not respect external WHERE filters unless those filters are applied upstream to the underlying rental data before aggregation; applying row-level filters after this view will not change the precomputed counts and min/max dates. | Do not use it when you need to deduplicate or count distinct customer rentals (for example count of unique customers who rented a film). The view uses COUNT(r.rental_id) and therefore counts rental transactions, not distinct customers or other distinct keys; reusing it for unique-customer metrics will miscount. | Do not use it when you need a different ranking behavior (for example DENSE_RANK, ROW_NUMBER, ascending order, or partitioned ranks by store/category). The view’s rentals_rank is RANK() over the global ordering by rental_count DESC; reusing it for partitioned or alternate ranking semantics will be incorrect. | Do not reuse this view if joins or filters upstream change the inventory->film relationship (for example if you need to restrict to a subset of inventory rows). The view aggregates by inv.film_id after joining inventory; altering inventory rows externally without recomputing will cause mismatches. | Do not rely on this view to identify films with zero rentals. Films with no rentals do not appear because the inner query starts from rental joined to inventory; reusing it to represent the full set of films (including zero-rental films) will silently omit those films.
params.comparison: use film_rental_counts(AGG) instead when you need the same per-film rental totals but with a different aggregation method or additional precomputed breakdowns — it likely computes comparable counts but may include alternative deduplication or filtering; prefer film_rental_counts if you must rely on its documented aggregation semantics. | use inventory_by_film_store(AGG) instead when you need per-film-per-store aggregates — ranked_films_by_rentals is aggregated only at film level, whereas inventory_by_film_store exposes the store dimension so you can compute store-partitioned counts or ranks. | use rental_enriched(JOIN) instead when you need row-level rental details (rental_date, customer, inventory) to apply custom cohorts, distinct counts, or time-window filters — ranked_films_by_rentals is already aggregated and cannot be filtered to change its precomputed counts/dates. | use film_basic(NORM) or film_category_join(JOIN) when you need film attributes (title, category) alongside counts — ranked_films_by_rentals only outputs film_id and rental aggregates; join to a film-level lookup if you need descriptive fields rather than reusing this view for joining without checking aggregation semantics. | use payment_by_customer(AGG) or customer_ltv_features(AGG) when your analysis is customer-centric. ranked_films_by_rentals is film-centric and will produce misleading results if reused to try to represent customer-level cohorts or monetary metrics.

views.description: Films ranked by rental_count with a dense rank. Exposes a rank column so downstream queries can select top-K films by rentals without embedding ranking logic. | Use for: Select top-N most rented films by filtering rentals_rank <= N; Compare ranks across time by reusing ranking CTE with time filters
